questions.question: The Himalayan Mountain ranges stretch in a west-east direction from the Indus River to which major Indian river?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Brahmaputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Himalayan Mountain range** is one of the youngest mountain ranges in the world, extending in a west-east direction from the **Indus River** in the west to the **Brahmaputra River** in the east.
 
• The **Brahmaputra River** originates in the **Angsi Glacier** in Tibet (China) and enters India through Arunachal Pradesh, flowing across Assam and Bangladesh before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• The Himalayas act as a natural barrier and determine the flow direction of rivers like the Indus, Ganga, Yamuna, and Brahmaputra, influencing the major river systems in India.
 
• The **Brahmaputra basin** supports diverse ecosystems and is crucial for agriculture, transportation, and water resources in northeastern India and Bangladesh.
 
• Both the **Indus River** and the **Brahmaputra River** are considered geographic boundaries marking the extent of the Himalayan range, making the Brahmaputra the eastern boundary. Hence, the statement is correct.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Himalayan Mountains:**

 
 
• The Himalayas are divided into three parallel ranges: **Greater Himalayas** (Himadri), **Lesser Himalayas** (Himachal), and **Shivaliks**.
 
• They are known for their geographic, climatic, and ecological significance, influencing monsoon patterns and river systems in South Asia.
 
• The Himalayas cover approximately **2,400 km** across five countries: India, Nepal, Bhutan, China, and Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Brahmaputra River:**
 
 
• The Brahmaputra is known as the **Tsangpo** in Tibet, **Dihang** in Arunachal Pradesh, and eventually Brahmaputra in Assam.
 
• It flows for about **2,900 km**, making it one of the longest rivers globally and a vital water source for millions.
 
• The Brahmaputra is prone to **seasonal flooding** due to heavy monsoons, impacting agriculture and settlements in Assam and Bangladesh.
 
 
 
• **Other Major Rivers Associated with the Himalayas:**
 
 
• **Indus River:** Originates in Tibet, flows through India and Pakistan, and forms the western boundary of the Himalayas.
 
• **Ganga River:** Originates from the **Gangotri Glacier**, flows through northern India, and is one of India's most sacred rivers.
 
• **Yamuna River:** A tributary of the Ganga, it originates from the **Yamunotri Glacier** and flows through northern India.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The Himalayas play a critical role in shaping the geography and hydrology of the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Rivers originating in the Himalayas are vital for irrigation, hydroelectric power, transportation, and drinking water.
 
• The unique climatic conditions created by the Himalayas significantly impact biodiversity and ecosystems in the region.

questions.question: Which military division had become rare in warfare during the Gupta period despite being part of the army in texts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chariot**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the **Gupta period**, the military structure of the empire included four main divisions as described in ancient texts: **Infantry, Chariots, Cavalry, and Elephants**.
 
• However, by the Gupta period, the use of **chariots** had become **rare**, as they were increasingly considered less effective in warfare compared to other divisions like cavalry and elephants.
 
• The decline of chariots in warfare was due to advancements in technology and changes in military tactics. **Cavalry**, which was faster and more mobile, had largely replaced chariots on the battlefield.
 
• Texts like the **Arthashastra** and other historical sources continue to mention chariots as part of the army, but their use was more symbolic or ceremonial during this period.
 
• The other military divisions, such as **Infantry, Cavalry, and Elephants**, remained prominent and were critical components of the Gupta military system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chariot Warfare:**

 
 
• Chariots were a significant part of ancient Indian warfare, especially during the **Vedic period** and earlier periods of history.
 
• They were primarily used in open plains where mobility and speed could be effectively utilized.
 
• By the **Gupta era**, advancements in military tactics and the development of better-equipped cavalry units rendered chariots obsolete for practical warfare.
 
 
 
• **Cavalry:**
 
 
• The **Gupta army** relied heavily on cavalry for its speed and mobility. Horses were easier to maneuver and could traverse various terrains more effectively than chariots.
 
• Cavalry units were equipped with **swords, spears, and bows**, making them versatile in combat.
 
 
 
• **Elephants in Warfare:**
 
 
• Elephants were a crucial component of the Gupta military strategy, used for their strength and ability to instill fear in enemy troops.
 
• They were often armored and carried soldiers equipped with **bows and spears** on their backs.
 
 
 
• **Infantry:**
 
 
• The infantry was the backbone of the Gupta military, consisting of foot soldiers armed with **swords, shields, bows, and arrows**.
 
• They were responsible for holding and defending positions during battles.
 
 
 
• **Symbolic Role of Chariots:**
 
 
• Despite their decline in practical use, chariots retained a symbolic role in **ceremonies and rituals**, representing power and prestige.
 
• They were also depicted in art and literature as a mark of heroic and divine figures.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Gupta Military Advancements:**

 
 
• The Gupta empire is renowned for its military organization, including innovations in **weaponry and strategy**.
 
• Their use of cavalry and elephants demonstrated a shift towards more **dynamic and effective methods of warfare**.
 
 
 
• **Decline of Chariots Globally:**
 
 
• The decline of chariots was not limited to India; it was a global phenomenon. By the time of the Roman Empire and later, chariots were largely replaced by cavalry.
 
• This change was driven by the development of saddles, stirrups, and other technologies that enhanced the effectiveness of mounted soldiers.

questions.question: Which crop is primarily associated with plantation agriculture in Kerala?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rubber**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Rubber** is the primary crop associated with plantation agriculture in **Kerala**, contributing significantly to the economy of the state.
 
• **Kerala** accounts for more than **90%** of India's total natural rubber production, making it the largest rubber-producing state in the country.
 
• The state's **climatic conditions**, such as high humidity, consistent rainfall, and warm temperatures, are highly suitable for the cultivation of rubber trees.
 
• Rubber plantations in Kerala are primarily concentrated in areas like **Kottayam, Pathanamthitta, and Ernakulam**, which are known for their fertile soils and favorable conditions.
 
• Rubber is widely used in the production of **industrial goods** such as tires, footwear, and other latex-based products, making it an economically significant crop for the state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Wheat:**

 
 
• **Wheat** is a staple food crop of India, primarily grown in northern states such as **Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• It requires a **cool and moist climate** during the growing period and warm, dry weather at the time of harvesting, conditions not favorable in Kerala's tropical climate.
 
• Wheat is not a significant crop in Kerala due to unsuitable climatic and soil conditions.
 
 
 
• **Cotton:**
 
 
• **Cotton** is primarily grown in states like **Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Madhya Pradesh**, which have black soil suitable for its cultivation.
 
• It requires a warm climate and moderate rainfall, conditions that differ from Kerala's high-rainfall regions.
 
• Kerala is not a significant producer of cotton.
 
 
 
• **Rice:**
 
 
• **Rice** is another important crop in Kerala and is a staple food for the population.
 
• Rice cultivation in Kerala is primarily conducted in **wetlands** and is supported by the state's abundant water resources.
 
• Despite its significance, rice is not classified as a plantation crop, unlike rubber.
 
 
 
• **Plantation Agriculture:**
 
 
• Plantation agriculture refers to the large-scale cultivation of **cash crops** such as tea, coffee, rubber, and spices.
 
• These crops are grown for commercial purposes and often require significant investment and labor.
 
• Kerala is also known for other plantation crops like **tea, coffee, and spices**, in addition to rubber.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Kerala’s Climatic Suitability:**

 
 
• Kerala's tropical climate, characterized by **high rainfall** (200–300 cm annually) and warm temperatures, is ideal for rubber tree cultivation.
 
• The state has fertile, well-drained **laterite soils** that support the growth of rubber plantations.
 
 
 
• **Economic Significance of Rubber:**
 
 
• The rubber industry contributes significantly to Kerala's **GDP** and provides employment to thousands of people.
 
• It supports ancillary industries such as **latex processing and manufacturing** of rubber-based products.
 
 
 
• **Global Rubber Production:**
 
 
• Globally, rubber is mainly produced in countries like **Thailand, Indonesia, and Malaysia**.
 
• India ranks among the top producers, with Kerala being the leading contributor.

questions.question: In which of the following groups of states are the lower regions of the Western Ghats located where subtropical vegetation is found?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka**__.

__
 
• The **Western Ghats** is a mountain range located along the western coast of India, spanning several states including Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Goa.
 
• Subtropical vegetation in the lower regions of the Western Ghats is primarily found in the states of **Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka**, owing to their tropical climate and high rainfall.
 
• These regions are known for their rich biodiversity, including a variety of subtropical plants, trees, and wildlife. The Western Ghats is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** due to its ecological significance.
 
• The subtropical vegetation in these states consists of species like **teak, rosewood, and various medicinal plants**, which thrive in the warm and humid climate.
 
• Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka are located in the southern part of India, where the **Western Ghats' elevation and climatic conditions** support subtropical vegetation. Other states, such as Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, are not part of the lower regions of the Western Ghats where subtropical vegetation is prevalent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Western Ghats:**

 
 
• The Western Ghats is also known as the **Sahyadri Hills** in Maharashtra and Karnataka.
 
• It is one of the eight "hottest hotspots" of biological diversity in the world, featuring numerous endemic species of flora and fauna.
 
• The mountain range extends from Gujarat and Maharashtra in the north to Kerala and Tamil Nadu in the south.
 
• It influences the monsoon winds and serves as a critical water catchment area for peninsular India.
 
 
 
• **Vegetation in the Western Ghats:**
 
 
• The vegetation includes tropical rainforests, subtropical forests, and montane forests depending on the altitude and climatic conditions.
 
• Subtropical vegetation, particularly in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka, includes species such as **jackfruit, mango, teak, and rosewood**.
 
• The Western Ghats also host agricultural crops like **coffee, spices, and rubber**, which thrive in the region's climate.
 
 
 
• **Kerala:**
 
 
• Kerala receives heavy rainfall due to its location on the windward side of the Western Ghats, supporting lush subtropical and tropical vegetation.
 
• It is home to several national parks and wildlife sanctuaries like **Periyar Wildlife Sanctuary**.
 
 
 
• **Tamil Nadu:**
 
 
• The Nilgiri Hills in Tamil Nadu form part of the Western Ghats and feature rich subtropical vegetation.
 
• The state is also known for tea plantations and its biodiversity hotspots.
 
 
 
• **Karnataka:**
 
 
• Karnataka's Western Ghats regions, such as Coorg and Chikmagalur, are famous for coffee plantations and subtropical flora.
 
• The state's forests are home to endemic species and medicinal plants.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **UNESCO World Heritage:**

 
 
• The Western Ghats was designated as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012** due to its ecological importance and biodiversity.
 
• The mountain range is divided into 39 sites, including national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, and reserve forests.
 
 
 
• **Climate and Geography:**
 
 
• The Western Ghats' climate varies from tropical in the lower regions to subtropical and temperate at higher altitudes.
 
• The average annual rainfall in the Western Ghats ranges from **1500 mm to 3500 mm**, supporting diverse vegetation types.
 
 
 
• **Biodiversity:**
 
 
• The range hosts more than **7,400 species** of plants, animals, birds, and insects, including several endangered species.
 
• It is an important region for conservation efforts in India.

questions.question: Which sector was the dominant contributor to India's GDP immediately after independence in 1947?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **1947**, immediately after **India's independence**, the economy was predominantly agrarian. **Agriculture** was the most significant contributor to the nation's **GDP**, accounting for over **50%** of the total GDP.
 
• The majority of the Indian population, approximately **70%**, was directly or indirectly engaged in agricultural activities, making it the backbone of the economy.
 
• India's agricultural sector was largely dependent on traditional farming methods, with limited mechanization and reliance on monsoons for irrigation.
 
• Industrial and service sectors were relatively underdeveloped at the time. Industrialization was in its nascent stage, and services like trade and finance catered to a smaller segment of society.
 
• The colonial policies of the British had adversely impacted the agricultural sector, leading to stagnation in productivity and rural poverty. Despite this, agriculture remained the primary livelihood source for the majority of the population.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Agriculture in Post-Independence India:**

 
 
• Agriculture relied heavily on traditional practices such as **bullock-driven ploughs**, manual sowing, and harvesting.
 
• **Food insecurity** was a significant issue due to low agricultural productivity, leading to frequent famines and dependence on food imports like the **PL-480 scheme** from the United States.
 
• Key challenges included lack of irrigation facilities, poor infrastructure, and fragmented landholdings, which hindered large-scale farming.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Sector:**
 
 
• The industrial sector contributed a smaller percentage to the GDP in 1947, with industries primarily focused on **textiles, jute, and iron and steel**.
 
• Post-independence, the government took initiatives to boost industrialization through **Five-Year Plans** and the establishment of public sector enterprises.
 
 
 
• **Service Sector:**
 
 
• The services sector, including trade, finance, and education, was not a significant contributor to GDP at the time of independence.
 
• With time, the sector grew due to increased urbanization and investment in infrastructure, becoming a dominant contributor to GDP in the following decades.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• India's first **Five-Year Plan (1951-56)** focused heavily on agriculture and irrigation to address food shortages and improve productivity.
 
• The **Green Revolution** in the 1960s significantly transformed the agricultural landscape, enhancing productivity and reducing dependency on food imports.
 
• By the **1990s**, the share of agriculture in GDP began to decline as the industrial and service sectors grew rapidly.

• ***Hence, the correct answer is Microphone – Input device, Monitor – Output device.***

questions.question: During the colonial period in India, the Vernacular Press Act (1878) was introduced by _____.
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Vernacular Press Act** was introduced in **1878** by **Lord Lytton**, who served as the Viceroy of India from 1876 to 1880.
 
• This act was specifically targeted at suppressing the freedom of the **Indian-language press**, which was critical of British policies and governance in India.
 
• The act empowered the government to confiscate printing presses, materials, and publications if they were found to be publishing materials deemed seditious.
 
• The act was widely criticized for being draconian and suppressive, as it was designed to curb dissent and prevent the Indian press from expressing nationalist ideas.
 
• It excluded the English-language press, showcasing the discriminatory nature of the legislation and the colonial government's intent to suppress indigenous voices. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lord Lytton:**

 
 
• Lord Lytton was appointed as the **Viceroy of India** in 1876 by the British government.
 
• His tenure is marked by controversial policies such as the **Grand Delhi Durbar (1877)** to proclaim Queen Victoria as Empress of India and the implementation of the Vernacular Press Act.
 
• He faced criticism for his handling of the **Great Famine of 1876-78**, where millions of Indians died due to inadequate relief measures.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Vernacular Press Act:**
 
 
• The act was seen as an attack on the freedom of expression and a tool to control the growing wave of nationalism in India.
 
• It led to widespread resentment among Indians, who viewed it as a blatant attempt to silence their voices.
 
• The act intensified the demand for freedom of the press and contributed to the political awakening of Indians against colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Other Colonial Acts Related to Press:**
 
 
• The **Press Act of 1910** was another restrictive legislation aimed at curbing nationalist sentiments through the press.
 
• Later, the **Indian Press Act of 1931** imposed further restrictions due to the rise of revolutionary movements and nationalist activities.
 
• These acts collectively highlight the colonial government's efforts to suppress dissent and control public opinion in India.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Vernacular Press Act:**
 
 
• The act fueled the nationalist movement, as leaders and activists began to demand greater freedom and rights for Indians.
 
• It led to the emergence of underground publications and alternative ways of spreading nationalist ideas.
 
• Eventually, the press played a crucial role in India's struggle for independence, highlighting the importance of freedom of expression in colonial India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Lord Curzon:**

 
 
• He served as the **Viceroy of India** from 1899 to 1905.
 
• Lord Curzon is known for the controversial **Partition of Bengal in 1905**, aimed at dividing Hindus and Muslims.
 
• He also focused on administrative reforms and the preservation of Indian monuments.
 
 
 
• **Lord Wellesley:**
 
 
• He served as the **Governor-General of India** from 1798 to 1805.
 
• Lord Wellesley is known for his **expansionist policies** and the introduction of the **Subsidiary Alliance** system.
 
• He played a significant role in establishing British dominance over Indian princely states.
 
 
 
• **Lord Ripon:**
 
 
• Lord Ripon was the **Viceroy of India** from 1880 to 1884.
 
• He is celebrated for his liberal policies, including the **Repeal of the Vernacular Press Act** in 1882.
 
• He introduced the **Local Self-Government Act** and is often called the "Father of Local Self-Government in India."

questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Tenth Schedule** of the Indian Constitution was added by the **52nd Amendment Act of 1985** and is popularly known as the **Anti-Defection Law**.
 
• It contains provisions to prevent **political defection** by Members of Parliament (MPs) and Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs).
 
• The primary aim of the Tenth Schedule is to ensure **political stability** by discouraging elected representatives from switching parties for personal gains.
 
• Under the Anti-Defection Law, a member can be disqualified if they **voluntarily give up the membership of their party** or vote against the party's directive without prior permission.
 
• The decision regarding disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is made by the **Speaker or Chairman** of the respective House, whose decision is subject to judicial review.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Anti-Defection Law:**

 
 
• The **Anti-Defection Law** was enacted to address the issue of instability caused by defections by legislators after elections.
 
• The law applies to both Parliament and State Legislatures in India.
 
• A legislator is deemed to have defected if they **join another party**, abstain from voting on key issues against their party's directives, or voluntarily give up their party membership.
 
• Exemptions are made for merger cases where at least **two-thirds of the members** of a party agree to merge with another party.
 
 
 
• **Role of Speaker/Chairman:**
 
 
• The Speaker or Chairman of the House decides on disqualification cases under the Anti-Defection Law.
 
• While their decision is final, it is subject to **judicial review**, ensuring accountability.
 
• There have been instances where the judiciary intervened in cases of delayed or biased decisions under the law.
 
 
 
• **Challenges and Criticism:**
 
 
• The law has been criticized for not addressing the issue of internal democracy within political parties.
 
• It has been observed that party leaderships often misuse the law to suppress dissent within the party.
 
• Delay in decision-making by presiding officers has often led to political instability.
 
 
 
• **Significance:**
 
 
• The Anti-Defection Law plays a crucial role in ensuring the **stability of governments** and promoting loyalty to party ideologies.
 
• It prevents unscrupulous practices like horse-trading of legislators and unethical political alliances.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The Tenth Schedule was introduced in **1985** during the tenure of Prime Minister **Rajiv Gandhi**.
 
• The law has been amended several times to address evolving political challenges.
 
• Judicial review has emerged as a critical aspect of ensuring the proper implementation of the Anti-Defection Law.
 
• While the law has largely succeeded in curbing defections, critics argue that it needs further reform to enhance the democratic functioning of political institutions.

• The CBFC assigns certifications to films, such as **U** (Universal), **UA** (Parental guidance for children under 12 years), **A** (Adult), and **S** (Restricted to specialized audiences, such as doctors or scientists).
 
• The Board ensures that films adhere to the cultural, social, and legal sensitivities of the country and do not contain content that could incite communal disharmony or disrupt public order.

• **State Legislative Council Formation:**

 
 
• The **State Legislative Council** is established under **Article 168** of the Indian Constitution. Not all states have a Legislative Council; it exists in states like **Bihar**, **Uttar Pradesh**, **Karnataka**, and a few others.

• **Composition:**
 
 
• The Legislative Council's members are elected and nominated from different categories:

• The Legislative Council acts as a **reviewing body** for legislation passed by the Legislative Assembly.

• To abolish or create a Legislative Council, the concerned state assembly must pass a resolution by a **special majority**.

questions.question: Why is air transport less popular for freight movement in India?

options.text: It is widely available in rural and remote villages.
It requires minimal infrastructure for operation.
It is expensive and ideal only for light, high-value goods.
It is slower and less efficient than water transport

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **High Cost of Air Transport:** Air transport is significantly more expensive compared to other modes of freight transport, such as road, rail, or water. This high cost limits its use primarily to light and high-value goods like electronics, jewelry, and pharmaceuticals.
 
• **Suitability for Specific Goods:** Due to its cost, air freight is ideal for goods that are time-sensitive or perishable, such as flowers or medical supplies. This makes it unsuitable for bulkier, low-value commodities such as agricultural produce or construction materials.
 
• **Limited Accessibility:** Air transport infrastructure is concentrated in urban and metropolitan areas. Rural and remote regions in India lack the necessary airport facilities, making it an impractical option for freight movement in such areas.
 
• **Infrastructure Requirements:** Unlike other modes of transport, air transport requires complex and expensive infrastructure, such as airports, air traffic control systems, and advanced security measures, which further increases its operational costs.
 
• **Environmental Concerns:** Air transport contributes significantly to carbon emissions, making it less environmentally friendly compared to other modes of transportation. This further restricts its widespread adoption for freight movement in India.

• **Road Transport:** Road transport is widely used for freight movement in India due to its extensive network and ability to provide last-mile connectivity. It is cost-effective for short and medium distances.
 
• **Rail Transport:** Railways are cost-efficient for transporting heavy and bulk goods over long distances. India’s rail network is one of the largest in the world, making it a preferred mode for industries.
 
• **Water Transport:** Waterways are the cheapest mode of transport for bulk commodities. However, their usage in India is limited to specific routes like the Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers and coastal shipping.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Goods Transported by Air:**
 
 
• High-value goods such as **gold, diamonds, and other precious metals**.

• Time-sensitive products such as **pharmaceuticals and organs for transplant**.
 
• Electronics and luxury items like **smartphones, laptops, and branded accessories**.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Expanding Air Freight in India:**
 
 
• **Lack of Infrastructure:** Many regions lack airports or cargo handling facilities, limiting the reach of air freight services.
 
• **High Operational Costs:** The cost of fuel, maintenance, and skilled manpower increases the overall expense of air transport.
 
• **Regulatory Hurdles:** Complex customs and regulatory procedures can delay air freight operations.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives:**
 
 
• The **UDAN (Ude Desh Ka Aam Naagrik)** scheme aims to improve regional air connectivity and make air travel affordable for the masses.
 
• Development of **dedicated freight corridors** and modernization of airports to handle cargo efficiently.
 
• Incentives for using environmentally friendly aircraft and technologies to reduce the carbon footprint of air transport.

questions.question: Who is responsible for the administration of Union Territories like Chandigarh and Lakshadweep?

options.text: Elected Chief Ministers of the Union Territories

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The President of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The President of India** is responsible for the administration of **Union Territories (UTs)** under Article 239 of the **Indian Constitution**. This article clearly establishes that the administration of Union Territories is vested in the President, who exercises this authority through an administrator appointed by them.
 
• Union Territories like **Chandigarh and Lakshadweep** do not have the same status as states, and their administration is directly overseen by the **Central Government**.
 
• The President appoints an **Administrator** or **Lieutenant Governor** to carry out executive functions on behalf of the Central Government in these territories.
 
• Unlike states, Union Territories do not have full-fledged elected governments (with some exceptions like Delhi and Puducherry, which have special provisions). Hence, their administration is directly overseen by the **President of India** through appointees.
 
• The governance of Union Territories ensures that the **Central Government** retains direct control over strategically important or smaller regions that may not be viable as independent states.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Governance of Union Territories:**

 
 
• There are currently **8 Union Territories** in India: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli & Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir, and Ladakh.
 
• Among these, **Delhi** and **Puducherry** have legislatures and elected governments with limited powers, while the remaining UTs are governed directly by the **Central Government**.
 
• The administrators or Lieutenant Governors appointed by the President act as the representative of the Central Government in these territories.
 
 
 
• **Role of the President:**
 
 
• The President’s role in Union Territories is defined under **Article 239** and **Article 239A** of the Constitution of India.
 
• For Union Territories without legislatures, the President exercises executive powers through administrators.
 
• In territories with legislatures (like Delhi and Puducherry), the President’s role is limited to appointing the Lieutenant Governor and overseeing certain legislative and executive matters.
 
 
 
• **Exceptions in Administration:**
 
 
• In Delhi, the elected government has powers over most areas except police, public order, and land, which remain under the purview of the Central Government through the Lieutenant Governor.
 
• Puducherry has a similar structure but with less friction between the elected government and the central authority.
 
 
 
• **Important Articles of the Constitution:**
 
 
• **Article 239:** Provides for the administration of Union Territories by the President of India.
 
• **Article 239A:** Deals with the creation of legislatures or Council of Ministers for certain Union Territories like Delhi and Puducherry.
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• In **Chandigarh**, the Administrator is generally the Governor of Punjab, who acts on behalf of the President of India.
 
• In **Lakshadweep**, an Administrator appointed by the President oversees the governance and implements policies as per the directions of the Central Government.

• **Union Territories vs. States:**

 
 
• States have full-fledged governments with legislative, executive, and judicial powers, while Union Territories are under the direct control of the Central Government.
 
• Union Territories were created for administrative convenience, strategic purposes, or to protect the cultural and social uniqueness of small regions.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Union Territories were introduced in the **Constitution of India** to administer areas that could not be merged with existing states due to their unique geographical, cultural, or political characteristics.
 
• The concept was inspired by the need to manage smaller regions or territories that were not viable as independent states.

questions.question: What is the preferred unit used in the scientific literature to express the ratio between two sound intensities?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Decibels**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Decibels (dB)** are the preferred unit for expressing the **ratio between two sound intensities**. It is widely used in scientific literature, acoustics, and engineering fields.
 
• The decibel scale is **logarithmic**, meaning a small change in decibels represents a significant change in sound intensity. It helps in expressing very large or very small ratios conveniently.
 
• Decibels are calculated using the formula: **10 × log10(P2/P1)**, where P2 and P1 represent two sound intensities or powers.
 
• This unit is commonly used for measuring **sound levels, electrical power, and signal strength**, making it versatile across multiple scientific domains.
 
• Decibels simplify the representation of sound levels, where 0 dB is the threshold of hearing, and values like 120 dB represent sounds at the threshold of pain.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Phon:**

 
 
• **Phon** is a unit used to measure the **perceived loudness** of sound by humans. It accounts for the sensitivity of the human ear to different frequencies but is not typically used in calculating sound intensity ratios.
 
• The phon scale is based on comparisons to a reference tone of 1 kHz.
 
 
 
• **Pascal:**
 
 
• **Pascal (Pa)** is the SI unit of pressure. It is used to measure the **pressure exerted by sound waves**, not the ratio between two sound intensities.
 
• For sound, pressure levels are expressed in micropascals (μPa), but this is more relevant to physical pressure than intensity ratios.
 
 
 
• **Hertz:**
 
 
• **Hertz (Hz)** is the SI unit for frequency, representing the number of cycles of a sound wave per second. It is used to describe the pitch of a sound, not the intensity.
 
• Frequency ranges like 20 Hz to 20 kHz are considered the audible range for humans.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Decibels:**
 
 
• Decibels are widely used in acoustics to measure **sound pressure levels** and noise pollution.
 
• They are also employed in electronics to express **signal-to-noise ratios**, amplifier gains, and attenuation.
 
• In telecommunications, decibels are used to quantify **signal power** and transmission loss.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Logarithmic Nature:**

 
 
• The logarithmic nature of decibels enables efficient representation of very large or small sound intensity ratios.
 
• It also reflects human perception of sound, where doubling the sound intensity does not equate to doubling the perceived loudness.
 
 
 
• **Thresholds:**
 
 
• The threshold of hearing is approximately **0 dB**, while the threshold of pain is around **120 dB**.
 
• Common sound levels include **60 dB** for normal conversation and **90 dB** for heavy traffic noise.
 
 
 
• **Decibels in Other Fields:**
 
 
• In electrical engineering, decibels express the **power gain** of amplifiers or attenuation of filters.
 
• In telecommunications, they measure **signal loss or gain** during transmission.

• The **Meter Convention**, also known as the **Convention of the Metre**, was signed on **20 May 1875** by seventeen countries.
 
• This international treaty established the framework for global collaboration in the science of measurement and the development of the metric system.
 
• The **Department of Consumer Affairs, Government of India**, celebrated the **150th anniversary** of the Meter Convention on **20 May 2025**.

• **Meter Convention:**

 
 
• The Meter Convention was signed in **1875** in Paris, France. It laid the foundation for standardizing measurements globally.
 
• The treaty originally focused on the metric system, but today it covers a broader range of measurements including mass, length, time, temperature, and more.
 
 
 
• **International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM):**

• It provides a platform for member states to discuss and develop global measurement standards.

• **Metric System:**
 
 
• The metric system is a decimal-based system of measurement used globally in science, engineering, and everyday life.
 
• Units like the **meter** for length, **kilogram** for mass, and **second** for time are part of the system.
 
 
 
• **World Metrology Day:**
 
 
• **20 May** is celebrated annually as World Metrology Day to commemorate the signing of the Meter Convention.
 
• The theme for World Metrology Day changes each year to highlight advancements in metrology and its applications.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Standardization:**

• They facilitate international collaboration and compatibility in various industries.

• The **Meter Convention** initially had 17 member countries, but today it has expanded to include **over 100 member states.**
 
• India became a signatory to the Meter Convention on **27 May 1957** and has actively participated in global metrology initiatives.
 
• The **metric system** has become the universal standard, simplifying international trade and communication.
 
• Celebrating the **150th anniversary** emphasizes the historical significance and ongoing relevance of the Meter Convention in modern times.

__
 
• The western coastal plains of India are classified as a **submerged coast**, formed due to the submergence of landmass below sea level.
 
• This type of coastline is characterized by **narrow plains** and the absence of significant elevation. The western coastal plains stretch along the **Arabian Sea**.
 
• The submergence has led to the creation of features such as **estuaries**, which are common along the western coast. Examples include the estuaries of rivers like **Narmada, Mahi, and Tapi**.
 
• Submerged coasts often have **deep natural harbors**, making them favorable for ports and maritime activities. **Mumbai**, a prominent port city, is an example located along the western coast.
 
• This coastal region is divided into **Konkan, Karnataka, and Kerala coasts**, each with unique geographical features influenced by submergence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tectonic Coast:**

 
 
• These coasts are formed due to tectonic activities such as **faulting, folding, or volcanic eruptions**.
 
• Tectonic coasts often exhibit features like **elevated shorelines**, cliffs, and platforms. An example is the coasts formed near tectonic plate boundaries, such as the **Pacific Ring of Fire**.
 
• The western coastal plains are not tectonic in nature, as they have been shaped by submergence rather than tectonic movements.
 
 
 
• **Volcanic Coast:**
 
 
• Volcanic coasts are formed due to the deposition of **lava and ash from volcanic eruptions**.
 
• Examples include the coasts of volcanic islands such as **Hawaii** or the **Icelandic coast**.
 
• The western coastal plains are not volcanic; no significant volcanic activity has shaped their formation.
 
 
 
• **Emergent Coast:**
 
 
• Emergent coasts are formed when land is elevated above sea level due to **tectonic uplift or lowering of sea levels**.
 
• Such coasts often feature cliffs, wave-cut platforms, and raised shorelines. Examples include the **Chilean coast**.
 
• The western coastal plains do not exhibit emergent features but are rather submerged coasts.
 
 
 
• **Submerged Coast:**
 
 
• Submerged coasts, like the western coastal plains, are formed due to the sinking of land or **rise in sea levels**.
 
• They often feature estuaries and deep natural harbors, making them conducive for maritime trade.
 
• Submerged coasts are commonly found along passive continental margins, such as the **western coast of India**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Western Coastal Plains:**

 
 
• These plains are divided into the **Konkan Coast** (Maharashtra-Goa), the **Kannada Coast** (Karnataka), and the **Malabar Coast** (Kerala).
 
• They are narrow and have an average width of **50-100 km**.
 
• Prominent rivers like **Narmada, Mahi, and Periyar** form estuaries along this coast.
 
 
 
• **Natural Harbors:**
 
 
• The western coastal plains host important harbors such as **Mumbai, Mangalore, and Kochi**.
 
• These harbors are crucial for trade and economic activities in India.

questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Expand the brackets using the distributive property directly:

⇒ 7x² − 5x + 3x² − 6 + 14

Combine the like terms for x² and constants:

⇒ 10x² − 5x + 8

**∴ The correct answer is 10x² − 5x + 8.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Expression: x(7x − 5) + 3(x² − 2) + 14

⇒ Multiply x into (7x − 5) to expand the first term: 7x² − 5x

⇒ Multiply 3 into (x² − 2) to expand the second term: 3x² − 6

⇒ Substitute these expanded values back into the expression:

⇒ 7x² − 5x + 3x² − 6 + 14

⇒ Group the terms with x², x, and the numerical constants together:

⇒ (7x² + 3x²) − 5x + (−6 + 14)

⇒ Add the coefficients for similar terms:

⇒ 10x² − 5x + 8

**∴ The correct answer is 10x² − 5x + 8.**

**__Additional Information__**

Distributive Property

The rule states that multiplying a sum or difference by a term gives the same result as multiplying each term individually: a(b − c) = ab − ac.

Combining Like Terms

Terms with the exact same variables and exponents can be combined by adding or subtracting their numerical coefficients: axⁿ + bxⁿ = (a + b)xⁿ.

BODMAS Rule

Always follow the order of Brackets, Orders (powers), Division, Multiplication, Addition, and Subtraction when evaluating or simplifying any mathematical expression.
</p

The difference between the sum of digits at odd places and the sum of digits at even places must be 0 or a multiple of 11.

questions.question: 8 years ago, the age of a father was 20 years more than twice his son's age. After how many years, from now, will he be twice his son's age?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let F and S be the ages of the father and son. We will track the expression (F − 2S) over time.

8 years ago, F − 2S = 20.

Every year, both F and S increase by 1, so the expression (F − 2S) decreases by exactly 1 every year.

Current value of (F − 2S) at present = 20 − 8 = 12.

For the father to be exactly twice his son's age, the value of (F − 2S) must become 0.

The time required to reduce from 12 to 0 at a rate of 1 per year is exactly 12 years.

**∴ The correct answer is 12 years.**

When two equal distances are covered at speeds x and y, the average speed for the entire journey is given by the formula:

Average Speed = (2 × x × y) ÷ (x + y)

Here, x = 3 km/hr and y = 6 km/hr.
